asgRatings.title: Ongoing Assessment for Dr Todd Mitchell, Consultant Psychiatrist
asgRatings.name: Independent Consulting Doctors
asgRatings.commentary:
Dr Todd Mitchell is the registered provider and manager of an independent consultant-led outpatient psychiatry service for adults aged 18 and over. The service provides assessment, diagnosis and treatment for a range of general psychiatric conditions. It is registered to provide treatment of disease, disorder or injury, and diagnostic and screening procedures.
The service offered remote consultations and face-to-face appointments at 10 Harley Street, London. It operated on Tuesdays, Wednesdays and Thursdays from 9am to 2pm. Clinical care was delivered by the consultant psychiatrist. Administrative support was provided through arrangements with Harley Therapy.
We rated the service good overall and good for safe, effective, caring, responsive and well-led. The service had clear processes to assess referrals and manage risk, and patients received personalised care in line with relevant guidance. Patients gave consistently positive feedback about access, communication, involvement and the way they were treated. Governance arrangements were proportionate to the size and nature of the service and included audit, peer review, appraisal and risk oversight.
The provider should strengthen arrangements for people who require language support. The service did not have a formal system for professional interpreting, and family members had sometimes supported communication during consultations.
During the inspection visit to the clinic, the inspection team:
• Carried out an environmental tour of the site, including the shared reception area and the consultant psychiatrist’s office.
• Spoke with 7 patients.
• Reviewed 2 online feedback forms completed by patients using the service.
• Spoke with the consultant psychiatrist.
• Spoke with the remote administrative assistant.
• Reviewed 6 patient care and treatment records.
• Checked how prescription stationery was stored and managed.
• Reviewed information and documents relating to the operation and management of the service.
• Reviewed policies and procedures relating to the running of the service.
Our rating of safe stayed the same. We rated it as good. The premises were clean, the consultant’s office was furnished, well-maintained and fit for purpose. The number of patients on the consultant psychiatrist’s caseload was well managed. The consultant did not keep a waiting list. Patients told us the service was flexible regarding appointments and appointments ran on time.
Our rating of effective stayed the same. We rated it as good. The consultant psychiatrist delivered a holistic, recovery-oriented service, offering pharmacological and psychological interventions where appropriate. The consultant psychiatrist completed comprehensive mental health assessments on admission and considered relevant physical health needs. They developed personalised care plans with patients, which were regularly reviewed. Treatment and care were delivered in line with national guidance and best practice to support patients’ recovery and wellbeing.
Our rating of caring stayed the same. We rated it as good. The consultant psychiatrist treated patients with compassion, kindness and respect. Patients’ privacy and dignity were maintained through confidential consultations, private treatment environments, and by involving patients in decisions about their care. Patients were actively involved in care planning and risk assessment, and their feedback was sought to improve the quality of care and treatment provided.
Our rating of responsive stayed the same. We rated it as good. The consultant psychiatrist carried out comprehensive clinical, psychosocial and mental health assessments to develop personalised care plans that reflected each patient’s individual needs, preferences, values and recovery goals. Care was tailored and reviewed to ensure it remained responsive to patients’ changing circumstances.
Our rating of well-led stayed the same. We rated it as good. The consultant psychiatrist had the skills, knowledge and experience to carry out their role effectively. Governance was monitored through regular audits, patient record reviews and risk oversight processes. Findings were used to address shortfalls, monitor quality and support continuous improvement.

People’s experience commentary

Feedback from patients was consistently positive. People described timely access to initial appointments, reliable appointment arrangements and flexibility to move between face-to-face and online consultations.

Patients said they were treated with kindness, dignity and respect. They felt listened to and had enough time to explain their concerns. They said the consultant psychiatrist explained diagnoses, treatment options, medicines and potential side effects clearly, and involved them in decisions about their care.

Patients knew how to seek support if their mental health deteriorated. They described prompt responses to queries, including questions about medicines. They also reported that the administrative support was helpful and responsive.
asgRatings.narrative: The service is performing well and meeting our expectations.

keyQuestionRatings.name: Caring
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that the service involved people and treated them with compassion, kindness, dignity and respect.

At our last assessment, we rated this key question as good. At this assessment, the rating remains good.

topicareas.name: Independence, choice and control

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service promoted people’s independence and supported choice and control over care, treatment and wellbeing.

Patients were supported to make informed decisions. Patients told us the consultant psychiatrist explained potential risks associated with treatment options, including the possible side effects of prescribed medicines, enabling them to understand their choices and actively participate in decisions about their care. People could choose the pharmacy that dispensed their prescription.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Kindness, compassion and dignity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service treated people with kindness, empathy and compassion and respected their privacy and dignity.

Patients said they felt listened to, treated with kindness and respect, and involved in decisions about care and treatment. Feedback was consistently positive.

The consultant psychiatrist supported patients to understand and manage their care, treatment and condition. They were flexible and made reasonable adjustments to meet individual needs where possible.

Patients said the clinician explained treatment options, prescribed medicines, and potential side effects, enabling them to make informed decisions. Medication reviews were described as collaborative, with treatment adjusted where appropriate to meet individual needs.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Responding to people’s immediate needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service listened to and understood people’s needs, views and wishes and responded to minimise concern or distress.

Patients said appointments were flexible and generally ran on time. Requests for urgent contact were triaged and responded to as appropriate.

The service had clear acceptance and exclusion criteria and made clear that it did not provide emergency or crisis support. Referral processes sought the information needed to determine whether a person’s needs could be safely met.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Treating people as individuals

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service treated people as individuals and made sure care and treatment reflected their needs, preferences, strengths, backgrounds and circumstances.

The consultant psychiatrist took a personalised approach to care, ensuring that treatment options and decisions were tailored to each patient’s individual needs, preferences and circumstances. Records showed that different options and solutions were discussed with patients to support shared decision-making.

Patients told us the service was flexible and responsive to their needs. One patient said that if they experienced a crisis, the consultant psychiatrist would rearrange appointments to ensure they were seen promptly. Another patient told us they had been referred to a specialist when this was considered more appropriate to meet their needs.

The service accommodated communication preferences. For example, correspondence was sent by post when a patient preferred this to email.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce wellbeing and enablement

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The consultant psychiatrist had access to professional and peer support that supported their wellbeing and ability to deliver person-centred care.

The service was clinically led and delivered by a sole consultant psychiatrist. Appointment management, billing, marketing and general administration were provided through Harley Therapy.

The consultant psychiatrist attended regular meetings with professional peers and collaborating clinicians which supported their own wellbeing. These arrangements supported peer discussion, reflective practice, professional connection and ongoing development.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Effective
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that staff involved people in decisions about their care and treatment, provided advice and support, reviewed care and worked with other services to achieve good outcomes.

At our last assessment, we rated this key question as good. At this assessment, the rating remains good.

topicareas.name: Assessing needs

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure people’s care and treatment was effective by assessing and reviewing their health, care, wellbeing and communication needs with them.

The consultant psychiatrist completed comprehensive mental health assessments with each patient over 2 to 6 sessions after accepting a patient into the service. Assessments considered clinical, psychosocial, mental health and communication needs.

The service also offered pharmacogenetic testing using a cheek swab to provide information about genetic variability that could affect how a person processes medicines. Patients said the consultant psychiatrist took time to understand their individual needs when discussing diagnosis and treatment. Patients felt that their needs were assessed in a person-centred way.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Consent to care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service told people about their rights around consent and respected these when delivering person-centred care and treatment.

The consultant psychiatrist understood how to manage consent to care and treatments and gave patients information about this. Records indicated that all patients had provided their consent to treatment and this was clearly recorded.

The service had a consent form for remote consultations that explained the potential benefits and risks of telepsychiatry, the alternatives available, including face-to-face appointments or no treatment, and patients’ rights.

Patients told us they could choose between in-person and virtual appointments, depending on their preferences and circumstances.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Delivering evidence-based care and treatment

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service planned and delivered people’s care and treatment with them, including what was important and mattered to them. They did this in line with legislation and current evidence-based good practice and standards.

Care records showed that the consultant psychiatrist assessed immediate and ongoing needs and used relevant National Institute for Health and Care Excellence guidance. The service worked with GPs, NHS services and specialists to support physical health assessment and monitoring. For example, we saw records where the consultant psychiatrist had used his clinical judgement and referred an at-risk patient to perinatal services and a specialist team.

Patients could be referred for psychological interventions, including cognitive behavioural therapy and dialectical behaviour therapy. The consultant psychiatrist reviewed side effects and discussed whether patients wished to continue treatment or consider alternatives.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: How staff, teams and services work together

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked effectively with external healthcare professionals to deliver coordinated, person-centred care and treatment.

Care records showed communication and referrals involving GPs, psychologists and perinatal psychiatrists. Before prescribing or starting treatment, the consultant psychiatrist sought relevant medical history, test results and information about current medicines. Treatment was not started when essential information was unavailable and safe care could not be assured, and patients were signposted to more appropriate services to ensure safe care.

The service sought consent at each consultation before sharing consultation outcomes and prescribing information with a patient’s GP. Where consent was declined, the consultant psychiatrist discussed the risks and considered whether treatment could safely continue. The service audited compliance with its consent process.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Monitoring and improving outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service routinely monitored people’s care and treatment to continuously improve it. They ensured that outcomes were positive and consistent, and that they met both clinical expectations and the expectations of people themselves.

The service had audit systems in place so improvements could be made. For example, the consultant psychiatrist had recently reviewed clinical records for evidence of recorded consent, which demonstrated that consent had been documented in 100% of cases. The service also completed audits relating to patients who did not attend appointments.

Patients we spoke with said the treatment they received had positive outcomes on their mental health and overall wellbeing.

 

Where patients required specialist treatment not provided by the consultant, such as dialectical behaviour therapy, they could be referred to appropriate specialist services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Supporting people to live healthier lives

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service supported people to manage their health and wellbeing and maximise their independence.

The consultant psychiatrist promoted self-care and gave personalised advice about anxiety reduction, stress management, sleep hygiene and lifestyle measures. Individual risk factors were discussed and reflected in care plans. People were referred for specialist assessment where appropriate. For example, patients presenting with symptoms consistent with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder were referred to specialist services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Responsive
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
We looked for evidence that the service met people’s needs and treated people equally and without discrimination.

At our last assessment, we rated this key question as good. At this assessment, the rating remains good.

topicareas.name: Care provision, Integration and continuity

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service understood the needs of its patient group and worked with other providers to support continuity of care.

The service had arrangements to support continuity when the consultant psychiatrist was unavailable. Administrative support coordinated alternative arrangements and, where necessary, the consultant psychiatrist arranged cover through a suitably qualified psychiatric colleague.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in access

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure people could access care and treatment within appropriate timescales and referred them elsewhere when it could not meet their needs.

Patients described timely access to assessment and treatment. Appointments were arranged promptly and the service offered both online and face-to-face consultations.

The service took steps to ensure that patients received the right care from the right professional at the right time. Where a person’s needs were outside the service’s scope, the consultant psychiatrist referred or signposted them to an appropriate professional or specialist service.

The consultant psychiatrist demonstrated an understanding of the importance of providing equitable care and ensuring that patients were not disadvantaged because of protected characteristics or personal circumstances. Patients told us they felt respected and valued as individuals.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Equity in experiences and outcomes

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service sought to provide equitable care and positive outcomes for patients from different backgrounds and with different needs.

Patients said they felt respected, listened to and involved. Care was tailored to clinical, psychological and social needs, and referrals were made where additional or specialist support was required. The consultant psychiatrist was aware of the importance of an inclusive approach to care and adjusted the support they provided to ensure equity in people’s experience and outcomes, including offering longer appointments to those who needed more time.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Listening to and involving people

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made it easy for people to share feedback, raise concerns and participate in decisions about their care.

Patients knew how to provide feedback, raise concerns or make a complaint. They felt comfortable approaching either the administrative assistant or the consultant psychiatrist and could also provide feedback through an online link.

The service had received no formal complaints in the 12 months before the assessment. Patient feedback described the service as supportive, responsive and person-centred.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Person-centred Care

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service placed people at the centre of their care and treatment choices and responded to changes in their needs.

Patients’ immediate and ongoing needs were assessed through comprehensive, holistic and person-centred care. The consultant psychiatrist completed detailed clinical, psychosocial and mental health assessments and developed care plans around each person’s circumstances, preferences, values and goals.

We saw evidence of person-centred care in practice. Patients were actively involved in developing their treatment plans and were supported to make informed decisions about their care. The psychiatrist explored patients’ personal goals and where appropriate, family members or carers were involved in discussions with the patient’s consent. Follow-up arrangements were adapted to meet individual needs, and care plans were reviewed regularly to reflect changes in patients’ circumstances.

Patients said they felt respected, listened to and involved.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Planning for the future

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service supported people to plan their ongoing care and involved other healthcare professionals where necessary.

The consultant psychiatrist discussed patients’ long-term goals, preferences and concerns and considered these when developing and reviewing treatment plans. Records showed that care planning addressed immediate needs while supporting longer-term wellbeing, recovery and independence. Referrals were made where additional professional input was required.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Providing Information

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service provided appropriate and up-to-date information in formats intended to meet individual needs.

Patients said they received clear explanations about diagnosis, treatment options, medicines and available support. They could ask questions and discuss concerns. The service ensured information about local support, rights, complaints and access to care records was available.

The service reported that information could be provided in easy-read formats. Family members had sometimes supported communication where a patient did not speak English fluently.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Safe
keyQuestionRatings.commentary: We looked for evidence that people were protected from abuse and avoidable harm.At our last assessment, we rated this key question as good. At this assessment, the rating remains good.

topicareas.name: Infection prevention and control

evidenceCategory.commentary: The service assessed and managed the risk of infection. Staff followed infection control guidelines, including handwashing. Cleaning records were up to date, and we observed that all areas were clean, tidy and well maintained. Cleaning was provided by the building landlord, including infection prevention and control procedures. The infection prevention and control policy had been updated to support the safe delivery of services. Audits were reviewed annually.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Involving people to manage risks

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people to understand and manage risks holistically so that care was safe, supportive and met their needs.

Care records showed that patients’ risks were assessed at referral and reviewed during treatment. The consultant psychiatrist gathered relevant information to determine whether the service could safely meet each person’s needs. There were clear processes in place to assess whether patients could be safely managed within the service and what their risks were. People were given clear information about what to do in a crisis as the service did not provide emergency or crisis care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning culture

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had a proactive and positive culture of safety based on openness and honesty. Staff understood how to raise concerns and report incidents, and there were systems to investigate safety events and support learning.

There had been no reported incidents in the 12 months before the assessment. The consultant psychiatrist and administrative staff understood what constituted an incident, adverse incident or near miss and knew how to report concerns.

A sample of the Service User Incident / Adverse Incident / Near Miss Report Form and procedures were reviewed. This confirmed that the service had structured processes in place to document, report, and monitor incidents should they occur. The consultant psychiatrist attended monthly meetings with Harley Therapy senior management, where incidents could be shared and discussed. The consultant psychiatrist understood the duty of candour and had a policy in place.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Medicines optimisation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure medicines and treatments were safe and met people’s needs, capacities and preferences. People were involved when treatment changed.

The service did not administer medicines or store medicines onsite. It had systems for safe prescribing and secure management of prescription stationery. The consultant psychiatrist was the only authorised signatory for prescriptions.

Care records showed prescribing followed relevant national guidance. The consultant psychiatrist reviewed the effects of medicines on people’s mental and physical health, discussed side effects and alternatives, and worked with GPs and other professionals to arrange monitoring. We saw letters sent to GPs with patients’ consent, including for people prescribed antipsychotic medicines.

The consultant psychiatrist followed General Medical Council principles for prescribing when treatment was delivered online.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe and effective staffing

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service made sure there were qualified, skilled and experienced people who received effective professional support and development.

The service was clinically led and delivered by the consultant psychiatrist. Administrative support was provided through Harley Therapy rather than directly employed by the service.

The consultant psychiatrist was registered with the General Medical Council, held a current licence to practise and met appraisal and revalidation requirements. The consultant psychiatrist completed annual appraisals through the Independent Doctors Federation. The most recent appraisal was completed in January 2026, and revalidation was undertaken every five years in line with GMC requirements. Evidence of appraisal and revalidation was available for review.

The consultant psychiatrist maintained professional competence through ongoing Continuing Professional Development including participation in the American Board of Psychiatry and Neurology's Continuous Maintenance of Certification programme and regular review of professional journals. They were also fully licensed and board-certified by the American Board of Psychiatry. The consultant psychiatrist attended monthly peer review meetings with other psychiatrists to discuss clinical cases, share learning and promote reflective practice.

Mandatory training was up to date and included safeguarding adults and children and adult and paediatric resuscitation.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe environments

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service detected and controlled potential risks in the care environment and made sure facilities and equipment supported safe care.

The shared reception areas, waiting rooms and consultant psychiatrist’s office were clean, well maintained and fit for purpose. The office was on the third floor and the building had a lift for people with restricted mobility.

The provider conducted safety risk assessments. There were appropriate safety policies, which were regularly reviewed. They outlined clearly who to go to for further guidance. There were no clinical examination rooms. Where a physical examination was needed, people were directed to their GP. The landlord completed premises risk assessments, maintained fire safety arrangements and serviced equipment. Fire exits were clearly marked and an automated external defibrillator was available in the main reception area.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safe systems, pathways and transitions

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people and external partners to establish and maintain safe systems of care. It supported continuity when people moved between services.

The service had clear operational boundaries and accepted people whose needs could be safely met in a non-acute outpatient setting. It did not provide emergency or crisis care. Exclusion criteria included acute or crisis presentations, active substance use, court-ordered treatment and people requiring immediate intervention.

Referrals included self-referrals and referrals from professional colleagues and psychotherapists. The service did not accept walk-in (drop-in) patients or referrals from medical services. People whose needs were outside the scope of the service were signposted or referred to appropriate specialist services.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Safeguarding

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with people and healthcare partners to understand and manage safeguarding risks. It protected people’s right to live in safety, free from abuse, discrimination, avoidable harm and neglect.

The service had systems to safeguard adults and children from abuse. The safeguarding policy had been updated in February 2026. The consultant psychiatrist and administrative staff had completed relevant safeguarding training and knew how to identify and report concerns. The service only assessed and treated adults aged 18 and over.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

keyQuestionRatings.name: Well-led
keyQuestionRatings.commentary:
This means we looked for evidence that leadership, management and governance assured high-quality, person-centred care; supported learning and innovation; and promoted an open, fair culture.

At our last assessment we rated this key question good. At this inspection, the rating has remained the same.

topicareas.name: Capable, compassionate and inclusive leaders

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The consultant psychiatrist had the skills, knowledge and experience to lead the service effectively.

The consultant psychiatrist maintained professional competence through annual appraisal, continuing professional development, peer review and revalidation. They demonstrated a caring and compassionate focus on patients’ needs and a commitment to keeping clinical practice up to date. Patients described the consultant psychiatrist as open and clear in their communication.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Freedom to speak up

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service aimed to create a positive culture where people felt they could speak up and their voice would be heard.

There were positive working relationships between the consultant psychiatrist, the remote Harley Therapy administrative team, and the premises management team at 10 Harley Street Ltd.

Staff described effective communication and collaborative working arrangements, which supported an open and positive culture where people felt able to speak up, share feedback and raise concerns. Staff were confident that their views would be listened to and acted upon where appropriate.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Governance, management and sustainability

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service had clear responsibilities, systems of accountability and governance arrangements that supported good-quality, sustainable care.

The service held regular monthly team meetings to discuss service delivery, governance matters and opportunities for improvement. The consultant psychiatrist had implemented a comprehensive range of policies and procedures to support the safe and effective delivery of care. These included policies relating to complaints, chaperones, infection prevention and control, controlled drugs, prescribing, safeguarding adults and children, data protection, governance, patient safety and consultancy arrangements. Policies and audits were reviewed annually to provide assurance that systems were operating as intended.

The consultant psychiatrist was aware of and had systems in place to meet the requirements of the duty of candour. They participated in an annual appraisal process through the Independent Doctors Federation, which included reflection on clinical practice, continuing professional development and personal development objectives. The consultant psychiatrist was supported to meet professional revalidation requirements and was allocated protected time for professional development activities, including appraisals, peer review and clinical audit. These arrangements supported professional accountability and provided assurance that the consultant psychiatrist maintained the knowledge and skills required for their role.

The consultant psychiatrist maintained a risk register to identify, monitor and mitigate risks within the service. Risks were regularly reviewed, and appropriate controls were implemented. For example, professional isolation had been identified as a potential risk and was mitigated through regular collegial contact with collaborating clinicians for case-based discussions six to eight times per year, active membership of professional networks, and regular consultative dialogues with the leadership team at Harley Therapy.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Learning, improvement and innovation

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service focused on continuous learning and improvement.

The consultant psychiatrist engaged with a range of professional networks and external organisations to support ongoing service development and maintain awareness of developments in mental health care.

The consultant psychiatrist participated in regular discussions with professional colleagues to reflect on clinical practice, share learning and consider developments in assessment and treatment approaches. This supported opportunities to consider different perspectives, identify improvements where appropriate and maintain awareness of emerging practice within the wider mental health sector.

The consultant psychiatrist also collaborated and consulted with other local clinicians and maintained links with specialist services, enabling the service to learn from wider professional experience and support continuous improvement in the care provided to patients.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Partnerships and communities

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service worked with GPs, NHS services and other specialists to support coordinated care and physical health monitoring.

Care records showed communication with specialist teams and other professionals. The service sought patients’ consent before sharing information with other healthcare providers and used this communication to support continuity and safe care.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Shared direction and culture

evidenceCategory.commentary: The service was led by the consultant psychiatrist, who was also the registered manager and registered provider. They worked closely with Harley Therapy, which managed the operational aspects of the service, to ensure patients received a high-quality, responsive and efficient service.The consultant psychiatrist and administrative support staff shared a commitment to delivering safe, effective and person-centred care. Effective communication between the clinical and administrative functions supported the day-to-day delivery of the service.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care

topicareas.name: Workforce equality, diversity and inclusion

evidenceCategory.commentary:
The service valued equality, diversity and inclusion and sought to ensure people were treated fairly, with dignity and respect.

The consultant psychiatrist understood the importance of equitable care and of responding to protected characteristics and individual circumstances. Patients said they felt respected and valued as individuals.

topicareas.qualityStatementscore: 3 - Evidence shows a good standard of care
